texts.preamble: Sh. Mukesh Kumar vs Food Safety Officer on 4 September, 2021 In The Court Of Sh. Dinesh Kumar Sharma Principal District & Sessions Judge/ Food Safety Appellate Tribunal Patiala House Court, New Delhi Fsat No. 01/2021 1. Sh. Mukesh Kumar S/o Sh. Kishan Chand Nominee Kay Pan Fragrances Pvt. Ltd. B15, Building No. 2, Buland Shahar Road Industrial Area, Ghaziabad201001 2. M/s Kay Pan Fragrances Pvt. Ltd. B15, Building No. 2, Buland Shahar Road Industrial Area, Ghaziabad201001 Both Through Ar Sh. Gyanendra Singh ...Appellants Versus Food Safety Officer Department of Food Safety Govt. of Nct of Delhi 8th Floor, Mayur Bhawan Connaught Place New Delhi110001 ...Respondent Date of filing of appeal : 24.03.2021 Date of arguments : 02.09.2021 Date of judgment : 04.09.2021 Fsat No. 01/2021 Page 1 of 10 Mukesh Kumar & Anr. Vs. Fso Judgment
texts.facts: The facts in brief are that on 13.10.2016, Sh. Bal Mukund, Food Safety Officer took a sample of 'Pan Masala' for analysis from Sh. Pawan Kumar Madan S/o Late Sh. Krishan Lal, M/s Pawan Store, 2632/30, Shadi Kham Pur, West Patel Nagar, New Delhi110008. The sample consisted of 12x189 Sh. Mukesh Kumar vs Food Safety Officer on 4 September, 2021 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/198673385/ 1 gm. sealed plastic pouches of Pan Masala (Ready for Sale), which was originally in sealed condition having declaration on it. One counterpart of the sample was sent by the FSO to Food Analyst, Delhi situated at Lawrence Road Industrial Area. 3. The Food Analyst vide Report No. FSS/481/2016 dated 22.10.2016 reported the sample to be misbranded on two counts. First, violation of Regulation No. 2.2.2.5(ii)(b) of the Food Safety and Standards (Packaging and Labelling) Regulations, 2011 read with Regulation No. 3.1.10(i) of the Mukesh Kumar & Anr. Vs. FSO Food Safety and Standards (Food Products Standards and Food Additives) Regulations, 2011, as declaration of the flavouring agent was not written on the package, as per the Regulations. Secondly, violation of Regulation No. 2.2.2(10) of the FSS (Packaging and Labelling) Regulations, 2011, as the word "within" was printed on the package in the statement with respect to Best Before Date. It has been stated that the appellants filed the reply, however, the same was not considered by the Ld. Adjudicating Officer in judicial manner.
texts.arguments: 5. Sh. Kundan Lal, Ld. Chief PP for the respondent has submitted that the Ld. AO/ADM has rightly imposed the penalties upon the appellants because the sample of the article was found to be misbranded, as in the lebel of the sample, relevant Regulations were not complied with. Ld. Chief PP for the respondent has also filed brief written submissions, wherein he has relied upon Regulation No. 2.2.2.5(ii)(b) of the Food Safety and Standards (Packaging & Labelling), Regulations, 2011, which deals with the declaration regarding food additives. It has also been submitted in the written submission that the appellants did not Mukesh Kumar & Anr. Vs. FSO mention the name of added flavour on the label of the sample. Moreover, the language of the label was also not according to the Regulation No. 2.2.2.5 of the Food Safety and Standards (Packaging and Labelling) Regulations, 2011 of the FSS Act, 2006. 6. Per contra, Sh. R.K. Ahuja, Ld. Counsel for the appellants has submitted that the complaint was filed against the nominee of the company and the company only on the basis of label declaration and that the invoice was not issued by the FBO i.e. Sh. Pawan Kumar Madan, M/s Pawan Store from where the sample of 'Pan Masala' was taken by the FSO. It has further been submitted that the FBO failed to produce any invoice of purchase of the sample. It has further been submitted that there is no evidence on the record that the appellant company has actually manufactured and supplied the article to the FBO and, therefore, the Ld. AO/ADM should not have imposed penalty upon the appellants/company. It has further been submitted that the genuineness of label cannot be presumed merely on the basis of label declaration and rather the invoice of purchase is required. It has further been submitted that the Ld. AO/ADM has passed the order without considering and examining various other points raised by the appellants. It has further been submitted that the sample has not been tested in a valid laboratory. Ld. Counsel for the Mukesh Kumar & Anr. Vs. FSO appellants has relied upon the following judgments: i. Kishore Kumar Vs. State of Madhya Pradesh, 2009 (2) FAC 333; Sh. Mukesh Kumar vs Food Safety Officer on 4 September, 2021 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/198673385/ 2 ii. Mukesh Kumar & Anr. Vs. FSO (5) Declaration regarding Food Additives. Functional classes for food additives shall be declared together with the specific name(s) or recognized International Numbering System (INS) as specified in Food Safety and Standards (Food Product Standards and Food Additives) Regulations, 2011 in the list of the ingredients; (a) Every food to which a flavouring agent is added in accordance with the Regulation 3.3.1(1) of Food Safety Standards (Food Product Standards and Food Additives) Regulations, 2011, it shall be declared in the list of ingredients provided that: i) In case of artificial flavouring substances the common name of the flavour shall be declared; ii) In case of natural flavouring substances or nature identical substances the class name of flavours shall be declared. 9. Ld. Counsel for the appellants has also relied upon B.L. Kohli (Supra), wherein the Hon'ble High Court of Delhi placed reliance on Shyam Lal Vs. State, AIR 1968 All 392. In Shyam Lal (Supra), it was inter alia held as under: "It seems to us clear that the true rule of construction of a penal statute is that where the legislature evinces its intention to modify the law, in favour of the accused so as to reduce the rigour of the law in the light of past experience and changed social conditions so long as prosecution of the accused has not concluded by a judgment of conviction, the proceedings against him are regarded as inchoate and the law applicable to him would be the law as amended by the legislature. The Court trying Sh. Mukesh Kumar vs Food Safety Officer on 4 September, 2021 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/198673385/ 3 an Mukesh Kumar & Anr. Vs. FSO accused person has to take into consideration the law as it exists on the date of the judgment." In B.L. Kohli (Supra), it was inter alia held as under: "Reference was also made by their Lordships to certain observations appearing in Rattan Lal v. The State of Punjab, AIR 1965 SC 444, wherein it was held that an ex post facto law which only modifies the rigour of a criminal law would operate retrospectively. Yet another authority of our High Court Municipal Corporation of Delhi v. Mai Ram @ Bhaya Ram, 1974 FAC 19 had also followed the decision in Sunder Lal v. Municipal Corporation of Delhi (supra) and it held that the modification of a penal provision which diluted the rigour of the offence being beneficient in nature had to be construed retrospectively. Mr. B.T. Singh, Ld. Counsel representing the State did not cite any authority to the contrary and these authorities referred to above unmistakably help the petitioners." 10. 15. In the case of Nehrudasan Vs. Food Inspector, Madurai Corporation, Madurai, 2010(1) FAC 49, the Madras High Court in somewhat similar case of prosecution based on the contravention of Rule 32 of the Act referred to a decision of the same High Court in A. Rajasingh & Ors. Vs. The Food Inspector, 2008(1) FAC 172 wherein it was held as under: Sh. Mukesh Kumar vs Food Safety Officer on 4 September, 2021 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/198673385/ 4 "Prevention of Food Adulteration Rules, 1955, Rule 32(i) Packet of food product/Wheat AttaMisbranding by use of term "best within four months" instead of "best before ...." Effect Even though terminology found in both terms differ in appearance, actually no consumer would be misguided if he happens to see term "best within four months"Absence of words "best before four months..." and use of words "best within four months" would not in any way mislead consumer, and by no stretch of imagination could be termed as Mukesh Kumar & Anr. Vs. FSO misbranding of product It is to be seen that product is not adulterated and only allegation of misbranding is there". 16. In another case titled T. Prabhu & Another Vs. The State, 2007(1) FAC 314 also, the Madras High Court held that though the word "within" stands omitted after 01.09.2011, but by merely adding such word, the customers could not be said to have been misled or misdirected as there was no difference otherwise in the meaning conveyed. In another case titled Hindustan Lever Limited and Others Vs. Food Inspector, 2007(1) FAC 299, the Madras High Court held similar view on the label which contained the similar word as in the instant case i.e. "best before within 6 months from date of packaging". 11. It has been brought on the record that fresh Regulations came into effect in 2020 and the same has been duly notified. The other violation as alleged against the appellants also seems to be squarely covered in the judgment of Ram Babu Rastogi (Supra). 12. In Bhola Ram (Supra), it was inter alia held as under: "3. In the absence of a bill, cash memorandum or invoice in respect of the sale of any article of food given by a manufacturer or distributor or a dealer to a vendor, there could arise no presumption on the mere label or wrapper that the person purported to Mukesh Kumar & Anr. Vs. FSO be the manufacturer, distributor or dealer thereof is in fact such manufacturer, distributor or dealer. The bare word of the vendor in that regard would not be enough.
